notes:
I've written the notes below verse by verse, with a link after every point. Some of the sources you listed aren't covered, because I ran out of searches and page fetches before I could reach them:

- **Missing sources:** I found nothing from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, the Lutheran sites or Precept Austin's verse-by-verse page.
- **Popular modern teaching:** I found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace material on this psalm, so that section is left out.
- **Catholic and early-church views:** these come only from Augustine (on ccel.org) and the Douay-Rheims translation shown on Bible Hub.
- **Wesley's own notes:** I only saw his comments on vv. 3–4.

---

**v. 1 – "Who may abide in Your tent? Who may dwell on Your holy mountain?"**

*Traditional reading*
- Guzik says "abide" means being taken in as a guest in a tent. David is asking who can find shelter and provision under God's protection, not just who can visit the tabernacle. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-15/
- He thinks the psalm may come from when the ark was brought into Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-15/
- He says "dwell" is more permanent than "abide": a guest in God's tent versus a citizen of His holy hill. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-15/
- The Pulpit Commentary translates "sojourn" and says the tent and hill aren't meant literally. https://biblehub.com/psalms/15-1.htm
- Ellicott takes the two verbs as meaning the same thing here. He paraphrases the question as asking what makes someone a true citizen of God's kingdom. https://biblehub.com/psalms/15-1.htm
- Spurgeon says that judged by the law alone, no mere human being can live with God, because nobody meets the standards that follow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/15-1.htm
- Poole notes that the psalm says nothing about ceremonies and rituals. He takes this as a correction to Israelites who relied on rituals too much, not a dismissal of them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/15-1.htm

*Where readers differ: what the "tent" stands for*
- **Gill (Baptist):** it is not Christ's human nature, and not heaven. "Sojourn" means lodging for a while, which doesn't fit heaven. The tent is the church on earth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/15.htm
- **Matthew Henry (Presbyterian):** the psalm shows the way to heaven, and the question is really "who shall go to heaven." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_015.cfm
- **Clarke (Methodist):** the tent is the church on earth (the "Church militant") and the hill is the church in glory (the "Church triumphant"). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-15.html

*Other views*
- **Augustine:** a tent is properly a soldier's shelter. Christians fight the devil for a time and need a place to rest, which points to faith in the Incarnation. The holy mountain may mean our eternal home. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf108.ii.XV.html
- **Maclaren (Expositor's Bible):** the psalm is not only about going to a physical tabernacle. The symbol is already giving way to the spiritual reality behind it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/15.htm

---

**v. 2 – walks with integrity, practises righteousness, speaks truth from the heart**

*Traditional reading*
- Maclaren sees "walks with integrity" as the overall demand, which is then split into right actions and truthful speech. The verb forms point to habits, not one-off acts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/15.htm
- Benson takes "walks" as describing a whole life lived without deceit, and "speaks the truth in his heart" as words that match what one really thinks and intends. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/15-2.htm
- **Augustine:** some people have truth on their lips but not in their hearts. Even saying something true is not enough unless the heart is true too. https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf108/npnf108.ii.XV.html

*Where traditions differ: law and gospel, faith and works*
- **Gill (Baptist, Calvinist):** "upright" means sincere, not sinless. Working righteousness is not done to earn justification; it means trusting Christ's righteousness and then doing good works as the fruit of that faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/15.htm
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** true faith shows itself in good works. Using an older writer, he says no work makes an unrighteous person righteous, since we are made righteous only by faith, with Christ's righteousness credited to us. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps015.cfm
- **Guzik (Calvary Chapel; enduringword.com, one of your Pentecostal/charismatic sites):** David speaks from the Old Covenant, where blessing depended on obedience. Under the Old Covenant a righteous life was the *condition* for fellowship with God; under the New it is the *result* of that fellowship, which rests on faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-15/
- **Clarke (Methodist):** he cites "the doers, not the hearers, of the law shall be justified." He also says much more is needed under the Christian dispensation than what is listed here. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-15.html

---

**v. 3 – no slander, no harm to a neighbour, no scorn on a friend**

*Traditional reading*
- Guzik: an upright life shows in how someone speaks, and he links this to Matthew 12:34. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-15/
- Gill: the Hebrew word for slander comes from "foot," picturing a gossip going from house to house. Not "taking up" a reproach means not starting a bad report, not listening to one, and not spreading one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/15.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says the ninth commandment (against false witness) comes first because breaking it is so common. It also notes the word "neighbour" in the middle line implies a closer friendship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/15-3.htm
- **Wesley:** "neighbour" means anyone. Not taking up a reproach means not starting it, not spreading it, and not believing it without good reason. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-psalms/
- Spurgeon: if nobody enjoyed hearing bad reports, nobody would spread them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps015.cfm

---

**v. 4 – despises the vile, honours God-fearers, keeps a costly oath**

*Traditional reading*
- Guzik: we cannot love good without opposing evil (Proverbs 8:13). The righteous person judges people by godly standards, not by favouritism or flattery. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-15/
- Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik): we should be as honest in giving people respect as in paying our bills. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-15/
- Matthew Henry: a wicked person's wealth or status earns no admiration, and a godly person's poverty takes nothing away from them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_015.cfm
- **Wesley:** "honoureth" covers godly people who are poor, and even those who differ "in some opinions or practices of lesser moment." https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-psalms/
- On the oath: Guzik gives Joshua keeping his oath to the Gibeonites as an example. He quotes Maclaren, who links "change" to the law forbidding a swap of a vowed sacrifice (Leviticus 27:10). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-15/
- **Wesley:** the oath is a promise. He gives the example of agreeing to sell an estate below its value and still going through with it. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-psalms/
- **Calvin:** keeping an oath when it works against your own interests is no small test of character. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/15-4.html

*Different readings of the Hebrew*
- **"Despised in his own eyes" (humility):** Gill reports that the Targum (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase) and the medieval Jewish scholars Ibn Ezra and Kimchi read it this way. Gill calls this "no bad sense" but prefers the usual reading. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/15.htm
- Ellicott and the Cambridge Bible reject the humility reading. They say the line contrasts despising the base with honouring the godly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/15-4.htm
- **"Swears to his neighbour":** the Greek Septuagint reads this, and the Anglican Prayer Book combines both ideas: he swears to his neighbour and doesn't let him down, "though it were to his own hindrance." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/15-4.htm
- The Catholic Douay-Rheims follows the same line: "sweareth to his neighbour, and deceiveth not." https://biblehub.com/psalms/15-4.htm
- Augustine reads it the same way. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf108.ii.XV.html
- Some Jewish writers took it as a vow to fast (Gill, who rejects this). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/15.htm
- Clarke reports that the Aramaic version reads "sweareth to afflict himself." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-15.html

*Baptist note on oaths*
- Spurgeon: under the New Testament, believers "swear not at all," but their plain word is as good as an oath. He also says Christ, our "Surety," swore to His own hurt and stood by it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps015.cfm

---

**v. 5a – no interest on loans, no bribes against the innocent**

*Traditional reading (broad agreement)*
- Ellicott: the laws against interest protected the poor among Israelites; interest itself wasn't seen as wrong. The Hebrew word means "bite." The parable of the talents shows interest in legitimate trade was accepted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/15-5.htm
- Barnes: what's forbidden is a harsh, grasping attitude that takes advantage of other people's troubles, not interest as such. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/15-5.htm
- Gill: moderate interest is no more wrong than charging rent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/15-5.htm
- Matthew Henry makes the same comparison with rent, but says a citizen of Zion lends freely to the poor. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_015.cfm
- Guzik, quoting Kidner: interest is condemned when it profits from a brother's misfortune. The verse is really about greed overriding justice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-15/
- The Pulpit Commentary: the bribe is one taken by a judge or witness against an innocent person. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/15-5.htm
- **Augustine:** these are "no great things." Someone who can't manage even these is much less able to speak truth from the heart. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf108.ii.XV.html

---

**v. 5b – "He who does these things will never be shaken"**

*Traditional reading*
- Maclaren: the ending goes further than the opening question. This person not only lives in God's tent but stands firm "though all the world should rock." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/15.htm
- Spurgeon: no storm will tear him from his foundations; he is not only *on* Zion but *like* Zion. He may be "moved" for a time, but never removed for ever. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps015.cfm
- Guzik: seeing how short we fall of this list should drive us to Jesus, who met all of it, so that by faith His obedience counts as ours. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-15/

*Where traditions differ: can a believer finally fall away?*
- **Reformed/Calvinist writers** read the promise as final perseverance:
  - Poole: he may stagger and fall, but will never finally fall away.
  - Gill (Baptist): he may fall into sin many times, but not totally or finally.
  - Geneva Bible notes: he will not be cast out of the Church as a hypocrite.
  
  All three: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/15-5.htm
- **Benson (Methodist):** these deeds flow from faith working by love, after justification and the renewal of one's nature. The promise is for the one who "steadily and perseveringly" walks in good works; such a person will remain in God's favour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/15-5.htm
- **Clarke (Methodist):** "the life of grace is the way to the life of glory." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-15.html

*Other views*
- The Cambridge Bible: under God's protection this person will enjoy "unshaken prosperity." This is a general statement and not linked to any prosperity-gospel teaching. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/15-5.htm
- Augustine notes the shift of tense: the earlier line ("the malicious one hath been brought to nought") is past, while this one ("shall not be moved for ever") is future. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf108.ii.XV.html
- The ccel.org editor adds that some Church Fathers called this psalm "the Ladder of Jacob," by which the righteous climb to God. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf108.ii.XV.html
